title: Cyber Security
summary: Malware families (virus, worm, trojan, ransomware), social-engineering attacks (phishing and cousins), preventive measures, and IT Act 2000 sections with CERT-In. Statement-based malware questions appear in nearly every CKT shift.

subtopics.title: Malware types
subtopics.concept:
**Malware** = malicious software. The family table:

| Malware | Behaviour | Spread |
|---|---|---|
| Virus | Attaches itself to a host file/program; corrupts data | Only when the infected file is run/shared |
| Worm | **Self-replicates across networks without any host file or user action** | Automatically over the network |
| Trojan (horse) | **Disguises as useful software**; opens backdoors, steals data | Does NOT self-replicate; user installs it |
| Ransomware | Encrypts the victim's files and demands ransom (WannaCry, 2017) | Mail attachments, exploits |
| Spyware | Secretly collects user activity/data | Bundled installs, drive-by |
| Keylogger | Records every keystroke (passwords, OTPs) | Often part of spyware/trojans |
| Adware | Forces unwanted advertisements | Freeware bundles |
| Rootkit | Hides deep in the OS with admin rights, concealing other malware | Exploits |
| Botnet | Network of infected 'zombie' machines under a attacker's control (used for DDoS/spam) | Worm/trojan infection |
| Logic bomb | Dormant code that fires on a trigger (date, event) | Planted insider/trojan |

WannaCry (2017) - global ransomware outbreak hitting unpatched Windows via the EternalBlue exploit - is the stock example question.

tricks.title: V-W-T triangle
tricks.body: **Virus needs a Vehicle (host file); Worm Wanders alone; Trojan Tricks you into installing.** Replication + host = virus; replication without host = worm; disguise without replication = trojan.

example.q: Which malware self-replicates without needing a host file?
example.solution: Worm.

tricks.title: Ransom = Ransomware
tricks.body: Encrypts your files, demands money -> ransomware (WannaCry). 'Keystrokes recorded' -> keylogger. 'Hides with admin rights' -> rootkit. 'Zombie army' -> botnet.

example.q: WannaCry (2017) was an example of?
example.solution: Ransomware.

mistakes: Saying a trojan self-replicates - only viruses and worms replicate; a trojan relies on disguise.
Saying a worm needs a host file - the worm is host-free by definition.
Calling ransomware a 'data thief' - its business model is encryption + extortion.
subtopics.notes:
### Malware — hostile software
**Malware** (MALicious softWARE) is any program written to harm, steal or spy. Exams test one skill: matching the malware's **behaviour** to its **name**.

| Malware | Signature behaviour |
|---|---|
| **Virus** | attaches itself to a file/program and spreads when that file is **run** — needs a host |
| **Worm** | **self-replicates on its own** across networks — needs **no host file** |
| **Trojan horse** | hides inside **useful-looking software** (free game, "update"); **does not replicate** |
| **Ransomware** | **locks/encrypts your files and demands money** (e.g. WannaCry, 2017) |
| **Spyware** | secretly **collects your information** and sends it out |
| **Keylogger** | records **every keystroke** — passwords typed are captured (a spyware cousin) |
| **Adware** | floods the screen with unwanted **advertisements** |
| **Botnet** | many infected "zombie" machines remotely **controlled as one army** (for spam/DDoS) |
| **Rootkit** | buries itself deep in the system, **hides its presence**, grants attacker admin rights |

### The three distinctions exams plant
1. **Virus vs Worm**: a virus rides on a host file and waits for you to run it; a **worm needs no host** — it crawls through the network by itself.
2. **Trojan vs Virus**: a trojan **never replicates** — it waits, disguised as legitimate software, and opens the door from inside (backdoor).
3. **Ransomware vs Spyware**: ransomware takes your files hostage for money; spyware takes copies quietly and leaves everything in place.

### How malware arrives
Infected email attachments and links, pirated software, infected USB drives, drive-by downloads from unsafe sites, and fake "your PC is infected" pop-ups. Once inside, malware may slow the machine, corrupt or delete files, steal data, or enlist the machine into a botnet without the owner noticing anything beyond sluggishness.

### Symptoms of an infected machine
Unexplained slowness, files renamed or missing, programs opening on their own, browser home page changed, sudden pop-ups, the fan and disk working when you do nothing. None of these proves malware alone — but together they are the exam's favourite scenario line.

### Quick revision
- **Virus needs a host; Worm needs none; Trojan replicates not.**
- **Ransomware = lock and demand money** (WannaCry 2017); Spyware spies; Keylogger records keystrokes.
- **Botnet = army of zombie machines**; Rootkit = hidden admin-level intruder.
- Malware spreads by attachments, pirated software, unsafe downloads.

patterns.name: Malware identification by behaviour
patterns.howToSpot: A behaviour is described ('self-replicates without a host', 'disguises as useful software', 'encrypts files for ransom') and the malware is asked.
patterns.logic:
1. Needs a host file = **Virus**; self-replicates alone over the network = **Worm**.
2. Disguised as useful software, does not replicate = **Trojan horse**.
3. Locks files and demands money = **Ransomware**; watches silently = Spyware/Keylogger.

example.q: A program that enters a computer disguised as a free game and does not replicate is a:
example.solution: **Trojan horse** — the disguise is its signature; replication belongs to virus/worm.

patterns.name: Ransomware scenarios
patterns.howToSpot: 'Files are locked and money is demanded', 'WannaCry' or any hostage-style scenario.
patterns.logic:
1. Encrypt-and-demand-money = **Ransomware** — the fastest identification in the topic.
2. Defence = **offline backups**; paying the ransom is never advised.
3. WannaCry (2017) is the named example exams use.

example.q: A hospital finds all its patient records encrypted with a demand for money to unlock them. This is:
example.solution: **Ransomware** — data taken hostage; restored from backups, not by paying.

patterns.name: Spyware, keylogger and adware
patterns.howToSpot: 'Records every keystroke', 'secretly collects browsing data', 'shows endless advertisements' — the quiet watchers.
patterns.logic:
1. Records keystrokes = **Keylogger** (passwords captured as you type).
2. Secretly gathers and sends your information = **Spyware**.
3. Throws unwanted ads = **Adware**. All three spy or annoy — none of them locks files.

example.q: Ravi suspects his typed passwords are being captured as he types them. Which malware fits?
example.solution: **Keylogger** — it records every keystroke, so even a strong password leaks.

patterns.name: Botnet and zombies
patterns.howToSpot: 'A network of infected computers controlled by an attacker', 'zombie machines used for spam/DDoS'.
patterns.logic:
1. **Botnet = many infected 'zombie' machines remotely commanded as one** — owners usually unaware.
2. Botnets are the muscle behind **DDoS floods and mass spam**.
3. The controller is the 'bot herder'; your slow machine may be someone's soldier.

example.q: Thousands of infected home computers are ordered together to flood one server. The infected network is a:
example.solution: **Botnet** — the army of zombies that powers DDoS attacks.

subtopics.title: Cyber attacks and social engineering
subtopics.concept:
| Attack | How it works |
|---|---|
| Phishing | Fake e-mail/site mimicking a bank or service to harvest credentials |
| Spear phishing | Phishing targeted at one person/organisation |
| Vishing / Smishing | Phishing by **V**oice calls / **SM**S |
| Pharming | Redirects users to fake sites by **poisoning DNS/host files - no click needed** |
| DoS / DDoS | Flooding a server with traffic; DDoS = Distributed, from a botnet of many machines |
| Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) | Attacker secretly intercepts/relays communication between two parties (open Wi-Fi sniffing) |
| SQL Injection | Malicious SQL typed into input fields to manipulate the database |
| Brute force / Dictionary | Trying every possible password / a wordlist of likely passwords |
| Social engineering | Manipulating humans (urgency, authority) - the 'human hacking' umbrella |
| Spoofing | Faking an identity: e-mail, IP, caller ID, website |
| Sniffing/Eavesdropping | Passive capture of network traffic |
| Identity theft | Stealing personal data to impersonate (Sec 66C IT Act) |
| Website defacement | Replacing a site's content (electronic vandalism) |
| Salami attack | Stealing tiny amounts (rounding offs) that accumulate large |
| Zero-day | Attack through a vulnerability the vendor has not yet patched |

tricks.title: The -ishing family
tricks.body: **Phi**shing = fake mail/site; **Vi**shing = Voice; **SMi**shing = SMS; **Phar**ming = fake site with NO click (DNS poisoned). If the victim 'entered a real-looking site without clicking any link', think pharming.

example.q: A fake banking site reached via a corrupted DNS entry is?
example.solution: Pharming.

tricks.title: MITM = postman reading letters
tricks.body: Man-in-the-Middle: both parties think they talk to each other; the attacker relays (and reads/edits) everything - classic on open Wi-Fi. Pure listening without relaying = sniffing.

example.q: Attacker secretly relaying messages between a user and the bank is?
example.solution: Man-in-the-Middle attack.

mistakes: Confusing pharming with phishing - pharming needs no victim click; DNS is poisoned.
Calling DDoS a single-machine attack - the D means distributed (botnet).
Believing strong passwords alone stop phishing - awareness + 2FA are needed; no password resists a fake site.
subtopics.notes:
### Attacks on people and systems
Beyond malware, exams list named **attacks** — methods of cheating users or breaking services. Group them by target.

### Attacks that target PEOPLE (social engineering)
- **Phishing**: a fake mail/site dressed as your bank or company, asking for passwords, OTPs, card details. "Phish" = fishing for victims with bait.
- **Spear phishing**: phishing **aimed at one specific person or office**, with personal details to look genuine.
- **Vishing** (Voice) and **smishing** (SMS): the same bait delivered by **phone call** or **SMS**.
- **Pharming**: even a **correctly typed URL** lands you on a fake site — the attacker poisons the DNS/server side.
- **Social engineering** is the umbrella: manipulating **people** (fear, urgency, authority — "your account will be blocked in 1 hour") instead of breaking code.

### Attacks that target SERVICES
- **DoS** (Denial of Service): flooding a server with useless requests so genuine users are shut out.
- **DDoS** (Distributed DoS): the flood comes from **many machines at once**, usually a botnet.
- **Man-in-the-Middle (MITM)**: the attacker secretly sits **between two parties**, reading or altering what they exchange (e.g. on open Wi-Fi).

### Classic named attacks from exam history
| Attack | Trick |
|---|---|
| **Salami slicing/salami attack** | stealing **tiny amounts from very many accounts** — paise shaved off, hard to notice |
| **Data diddling** | changing data **before or during entry** into the system (false figures) |
| **Logic bomb** | malicious code that **sleeps until a trigger** — a date or event — then detonates |
| **SQL injection** | typing database commands into a web form's input box to read the database |
| **Brute force** | trying **every possible password** combination until one works |
| **Eavesdropping** | passively **listening** to data as it travels |

### Telling the twins apart
Phishing asks the **user** to hand over data; pharming needs no user mistake — the **address itself is hijacked**. DoS asks nothing of users — it **drowns the server**. MITM does not flood or fake a site — it **listens in the middle** of a real conversation. Salami steals **small and often**; data diddling **alters records**; a logic bomb waits for its **trigger**.

### Quick revision
- **Phishing = mail bait; Vishing = voice; Smishing = SMS; Pharming = fake site despite correct URL.**
- **DoS/DDoS = flood the server** (DDoS from a botnet); **MITM = listen between two parties**.
- **Salami = tiny thefts, many accounts; Logic bomb = waits for a trigger; SQL injection = commands in a form.**
- Social engineering = attacking the person, not the machine.

patterns.name: Phishing family (mail, voice, SMS, pharming)
patterns.howToSpot: A fake-bank-mail / fake-call / fake-SMS / correct-URL-fake-site scenario asking for the attack's name, or 'vishing/smishing mean ___'.
patterns.logic:
1. Bait by **e-mail or fake site** = Phishing; by **phone call** = Vishing; by **SMS** = Smishing.
2. **Correct URL still lands on a fake site** = Pharming (address hijacked, no user mistake).
3. Aimed at ONE chosen person = **Spear phishing**. All are social engineering — attacking the person, not the machine.

example.q: A caller claiming to be from the bank asks for the OTP sent to Meena's phone. This fraud is:
example.solution: **Vishing** — voice phishing; a real bank never asks for OTPs.

patterns.name: DoS, DDoS and botnet floods
patterns.howToSpot: 'Server is flooded with requests and genuine users are shut out', 'attack from thousands of machines at once'.
patterns.logic:
1. Flood from **one source** = **DoS**; from **many machines at once** (usually a botnet) = **DDoS**.
2. The aim is **denial of service**, not data theft — the service drowns.
3. DDoS question almost always names 'distributed/thousands of computers' — that word IS the answer key.

example.q: A shopping site crashes as thousands of hijacked machines hammer it with fake requests together. This is:
example.solution: **DDoS** — Distributed Denial of Service; 'distributed' = many sources at once.

patterns.name: Man-in-the-Middle and eavesdropping
patterns.howToSpot: 'Communication between A and B is read/changed by a hidden third party', risks of open public Wi-Fi.
patterns.logic:
1. **MITM = attacker sits silently between two parties**, reading or altering the exchange — neither side notices.
2. Classic setting: **open public Wi-Fi** without encryption.
3. Defence: encrypted connections (**HTTPS/VPN**) — the middle man sees only ciphertext.

example.q: On free airport Wi-Fi, an attacker secretly reads the data exchange between Amit and the site he is using. This attack is:
example.solution: **Man-in-the-Middle (MITM)** — the hidden listener between two ends.

patterns.name: Classic named attacks (salami, diddling, logic bomb, SQLi)
patterns.howToSpot: 'Tiny amounts stolen from many accounts', 'records changed during entry', 'code that waits for a date', 'commands typed into a login box'.
patterns.logic:
1. **Salami attack** = many tiny thefts (paise from lakhs of accounts).
2. **Data diddling** = data changed before/during entry.
3. **Logic bomb** = sleeps until a trigger (date/event).
4. **SQL injection** = database commands typed into a web form; **Brute force** = trying every password.

example.q: A bank clerk's program quietly takes one rupee from thousands of accounts into his own. This is a:
example.solution: **Salami attack** — slicing tiny amounts off very many accounts.

subtopics.title: Preventive measures and security tools
subtopics.concept:
| Measure | What it does |
|---|---|
| Antivirus/anti-malware | Scans, detects, quarantines malware (Windows Defender - built-in; Norton, McAfee, Kaspersky, Quick Heal, Avast) - needs regular virus-definition updates |
| Firewall | Monitors incoming/outgoing traffic against allow/deny rules; hardware or software |
| Updates/patches | Close known vulnerabilities (WannaCry spread through unpatched systems) |
| Strong passwords | Long, mixed-case + digits + symbols, unique per site; avoid names/DOB; passphrase style |
| 2FA/MFA + OTP | A second factor beyond the password |
| Backups | Regular offline/off-site copies defeat ransomware |
| Encryption | Renders stolen data unreadable; HTTPS for web |
| VPN | Encrypted tunnel on public Wi-Fi |
| Digital signature | Verifies sender authenticity + message integrity (issued via Certifying Authorities) |
| Biometrics | Fingerprint/face/iris authentication |
| CAPTCHA | Human-vs-bot test on forms |
| Safe habits | Don't click unknown links/attachments; scan USB drives; avoid pirated software; log out; lock screen (Win+L) |

Antivirus is reactive/detective; a **firewall is preventive/gatekeeping** - exam options often swap their roles.

tricks.title: AV detects, FW decides
tricks.body: **Antivirus = detective** (scans files for malware already arriving); **Firewall = gatekeeper** (allows/blocks traffic by rules). 'Filters network traffic' -> firewall; 'removes virus from a file' -> antivirus.

example.q: Which tool filters network traffic based on defined rules?
example.solution: Firewall.

tricks.title: 2FA two doors
tricks.body: Two-factor = knowledge (password) + possession/inherence (OTP, token, fingerprint). One stolen password opens only the first door.

example.q: Password + OTP at login is an example of?
example.solution: Two-factor authentication.

mistakes: Treating antivirus as the network gatekeeper - that is the firewall's role.
Thinking updated antivirus alone guarantees safety - zero-days and phishing bypass it.
Writing passwords on sticky notes or reusing one password everywhere - both kill the 'strong password' measure.
subtopics.notes:
### The defence line-up
| Defence | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Firewall** | a barrier (hardware/software) that **monitors and filters traffic** between your network and the outside, by rules — allow or block |
| **Antivirus** | **detects and removes malware**, mainly by matching **virus signatures** — so it must be **updated regularly** |
| **Encryption** | scrambles data so only the key-holder can read it — **plaintext (readable) to ciphertext (scrambled)**; reading back is decryption |
| **Two-factor authentication (2FA)** | password **plus** a second proof — OTP on phone, fingerprint — so a stolen password alone is useless |
| **Backup** | a safe copy of data kept separately, so ransomware or disk failure cannot erase you |
| **Updates/patches** | fixes for newly discovered security holes — unpatched systems stay open doors |

### Firewall vs antivirus — the roles exams swap
A **firewall guards the doorway**: it watches network traffic in and out and blocks what breaks the rules — it does not clean infections. **Antivirus works inside**: it scans files and memory and removes malware that got in — it does not filter network traffic. A machine can have both, and each answers a different exam line: "which filters incoming/outgoing traffic?" = firewall; "which detects and removes viruses?" = antivirus.

### Encryption — the one diagram
**Plaintext** (HELLO) is fed with a **key** through an encryption algorithm to produce unreadable **ciphertext**; the receiver applies the key to decrypt. **AES** (Advanced Encryption Standard) is the widely used modern standard. When you see the **padlock and https://** in a browser, the web session is encrypted — the S means Secure. Encryption protects data even if it is stolen in transit; it is why open public Wi-Fi without HTTPS is risky.

### Password hygiene and safe habits
- Long passwords mixing letters, digits and symbols; **never name, birthdate, or 123456**; different password for each important account; changed periodically.
- **2FA everywhere it is offered** — the OTP is the second lock.
- Never share OTPs/PINs; banks never ask for them. Do not click links in unknown mails; download software only from official sources; keep the OS and antivirus updated; take backups.

### Quick revision
- **Firewall filters traffic by rules; antivirus finds and removes malware; they are not the same job.**
- **Encryption: plaintext + key = ciphertext; decryption reverses it; AES = the standard; https = encrypted web.**
- **2FA = password + OTP/biometric** — a stolen password alone fails.
- Backups defeat ransomware; updates close known holes.

patterns.name: Firewall purpose
patterns.howToSpot: 'A firewall is used for', 'which device/software filters traffic between networks by rules', hardware-or-software barrier statements.
patterns.logic:
1. **Firewall = rule-based barrier** between your network and the outside — allows or blocks traffic.
2. It **filters the doorway**; it does not scan or clean infected files.
3. Can be hardware, software or both.

example.q: The security system that monitors and filters data entering or leaving a network according to rules is a:
example.solution: **Firewall** — the doorman of the network.

patterns.name: Antivirus vs firewall roles
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which removes an infection already inside', odd-one-out items where one role is swapped between firewall and antivirus.
patterns.logic:
1. **Antivirus scans, detects and removes malware**, chiefly by signature matching — so **updates are compulsory**.
2. **Firewall filters traffic; antivirus cleans inside** — the swap is the classic trap.
3. Neither replaces the other; a protected machine keeps both.

example.q: Which tool detects and removes a virus that has already entered a computer?
example.solution: **Antivirus** — firewall could not have let it in if configured well, but only antivirus cleans inside.

patterns.name: Password hygiene and 2FA
patterns.howToSpot: 'Strong password' pick-the-best-option, 'two-factor authentication means ___', scenarios where a password alone failed.
patterns.logic:
1. Strong = **long, mixed (letters+digits+symbols), no name/birthdate/123456, unique per account**.
2. **2FA = password + a second proof** (OTP, fingerprint) — a stolen password alone is not enough.
3. Never share OTP/PIN; banks never ask for them — any such message is fraud.

example.q: Which of these is the STRONGEST password?
example.solution: A long mix of letters, digits and symbols unique to that account — not a name, birthdate or 123456.

patterns.name: Encryption basics (plaintext, ciphertext, AES, https)
patterns.howToSpot: 'Scrambled unreadable data is called ___', 'plaintext to ciphertext', 'the padlock/https means ___', 'AES is a ___'.
patterns.logic:
1. Readable original = **plaintext**; scrambled form = **ciphertext**; reversing = decryption, done with the **key**.
2. **AES** = Advanced Encryption Standard, the widely used modern standard.
3. **https + padlock = encrypted web session** — the S stands for Secure.

example.q: Data that has been scrambled so that unauthorised people cannot read it is called:
example.solution: **Ciphertext** — the encrypted form; plaintext is the readable original.

subtopics.title: IT Act 2000, offences and authorities
subtopics.concept:
The **Information Technology Act, 2000** is India's cyber-law framework - passed in 2000, **in force from 17 October 2000**, based on the UNCITRAL model law on e-commerce, and **amended in 2008** (adding 66C, 66D, 66F etc.).

| Section | Offence |
|---|---|
| Sec 43 | Penalty (up to Rs. 1 crore) for unauthorised access/damage to computer, data, virus injection |
| Sec 65 | Tampering with computer **source documents** - up to 3 years |
| Sec 66 | Computer-related offences (dishonesty/franchise of Sec 43 acts) |
| Sec 66C | **Identity theft** - up to 3 years + fine |
| Sec 66D | **Cheating by personation** using a computer (online fraud) - up to 3 years |
| Sec 66E | Violation of privacy (publishing private images) - up to 3 years |
| Sec 66F | **Cyber terrorism** - may extend to life imprisonment |
| Sec 67 | Publishing/transmitting obscene material electronically (first conviction up to 3 years + Rs. 5 lakh fine) |
| Sec 72 | Breach of confidentiality and privacy by a empowered body |

Note: **Sec 66A** (punishing 'offensive messages') was struck down by the Supreme Court in *Shreya Singhal v. Union of India* (2015) as unconstitutional.

**Authorities/portals:** **CERT-In** (Indian Computer Emergency Response Team, 2004, under MeitY) - the national incident-response and warning body; **NCIIPC** protects critical information infrastructure; **cybercrime.gov.in** is the national reporting portal and **1930** the cyber-fraud helpline (freezing defrauded money quickly).

tricks.title: Section story-line
tricks.body: **43** = damage fine, **65** = source code, **66** = computer crime, **66C** = identity (C for Credential theft), **66D** = cheating by personation (D for Donning a false identity), **66F** = terrorism (F for Fearsome), **67** = obscene.

example.q: Under which IT Act section is identity theft punished?
example.solution: Section 66C.

tricks.body: IT Act passed and effective in **2000** (in force 17 October 2000), UNCITRAL-based, amended **2008**. CERT-In follows in **2004**.

example.q: The IT Act came into force in the year?

tricks.title: Helpline 1930
tricks.body: Money lost to online fraud? Dial **1930** fast and report at cybercrime.gov.in - the hotline aims to freeze the siphoned money in the banking chain.

example.q: National cybercrime reporting helpline number?

mistakes: Saying the IT Act was enacted in 2008 - 2008 is the AMENDMENT; the Act is 2000.
Quoting Sec 66A as current law - it was struck down in 2015 (Shreya Singhal case).
Mixing CERT-In (incident response, MeitY) with NCIIPC (critical-infrastructure protection).
subtopics.notes:
### The Information Technology Act, 2000
India's law for the electronic world is the **IT Act, 2000**, in force from **17 October 2000**. It grew out of the **UNCITRAL model law** (United Nations Commission on International Trade Law) on electronic commerce, which recommended that countries give legal recognition to electronic records and signatures. The Act legalised **electronic records and digital signatures** and created punishments for computer crimes. It was **amended in 2008** (effective 2009), adding identity theft, cyber-terrorism provisions and the CERT-In mandate.

### Sections the exams keep asking
| Section | Subject |
|---|---|
| **Sec 3** | authentication by **digital (electronic) signature** |
| **Sec 43** | penalty/compensation for **unauthorised access and damage** to computer, data (hacking-type harm) |
| **Sec 65** | **tampering with computer source code** |
| **Sec 66** | **computer-related offences** — the "hacking" section (dishonest intent) |
| **Sec 66C** | **identity theft** (fraudulent use of password/digital signature/biometric) |
| **Sec 66D** | **cheating by personation** using a computer resource (fake profiles) |
| **Sec 67** | publishing/transmitting **obscene material** in electronic form |
| **Sec 72** | **breach of confidentiality and privacy** (by those with lawful access to data) |

**Section 66A** (punishment for "offensive messages") was **struck down by the Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015)** as violative of free speech — a favourite trick option presented as still-valid law.

### The watchdogs
- **CERT-In** (Indian Computer Emergency Response Team) — the national incident-response agency under **MeitY** (Ministry of Electronics and IT); set up 2004, statutory backing via Sec 70B after the 2008 amendment.
- **NCIIPC** (National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre) — protects **critical infrastructure** (power, banking, telecom) under Sec 70A.
- **MeitY** is the parent ministry for cyber laws and policy; the **DPDP Act, 2023** (Digital Personal Data Protection Act) now governs personal-data privacy alongside the IT Act.
- Reporting: national cyber-crime helpline **1930** and the portal **cybercrime.gov.in**.

### Digital signature in one line
A **digital signature** (Sec 3) is the electronic equivalent of a handwritten signature: created with the signer's **private key** and verified by anyone with the **public key** (Certificate Authorities issue the keys). It proves **who** signed and that the document was **not altered** — authentication plus integrity.

### Quick revision
- **IT Act 2000, effective 17 Oct 2000, based on UNCITRAL; amended 2008.**
- 65 = source code; **66 = hacking; 66C = identity theft; 66D = online cheating; 67 = obscenity**; 43 = unauthorised access penalty; **66A struck down 2015**.
- **CERT-In = incident response under MeitY; NCIIPC = critical infrastructure**; helpline 1930.
- Digital signature = private key signs, public key verifies (Sec 3).

patterns.name: IT Act basics (year, origin, amendment)
patterns.howToSpot: 'The IT Act was passed in ___', 'in force from 17 October 2000', 'based on which UN model law', 'the 2008 amendment'.
patterns.logic:
1. **IT Act 2000, in force 17 October 2000** — India's cyber law.
2. Based on the **UNCITRAL model law** on e-commerce (UN Commission on International Trade Law).
3. **Amended 2008** (effective 2009) — added identity theft (66C/66D), cyber-terrorism (66F), CERT-In backing.

example.q: India's Information Technology Act came into force on:
example.solution: **17 October 2000** — based on the UNCITRAL model law; amended in 2008.

patterns.name: Section-to-offence matching
patterns.howToSpot: 'Section 66 deals with ___', 'identity theft is which section', 'which section was struck down' — 43/65/66/66C/66D/67/72 and 66A.
patterns.logic:
1. **43** unauthorised access/damage penalty; **65** source-code tampering; **66** hacking (computer-related offences).
2. **66C identity theft; 66D cheating by personation; 67 obscene material; 72 breach of privacy.**
3. **66A (offensive messages) was STRUCK DOWN in 2015** — Shreya Singhal case. Any option using 66A as live law is wrong.

example.q: Under which section of the IT Act is identity theft punished?
example.solution: **Section 66C** — fraudulent use of another's password, digital signature or biometric.

patterns.name: Authorities: CERT-In, NCIIPC, MeitY, helpline
patterns.howToSpot: 'CERT-In stands for / works under ___', 'critical infrastructure is protected by ___', 'the cyber-fraud helpline number'.
patterns.logic:
1. **CERT-In** (Indian Computer Emergency Response Team) = national incident-response agency, **under MeitY**.
2. **NCIIPC** protects **critical information infrastructure** (power, banking, telecom).
3. Report fraud on **1930** or **cybercrime.gov.in**; personal-data privacy now also under the **DPDP Act 2023**.

example.q: CERT-In, India's cyber incident response agency, functions under which ministry?
example.solution: **MeitY** — Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology.

patterns.name: Digital signature and e-record legality
patterns.howToSpot: 'A digital signature is used for ___', 'which section gives digital signatures legal status', authentication/integrity statements.
patterns.logic:
1. **Digital signature (Sec 3)** = electronic equivalent of a handwritten signature.
2. It proves **who signed (authentication)** and that the document was **not altered (integrity)** — not secrecy.
3. Signed with the signer's **private key**, verified with the **public key**; Certificate Authorities issue the credentials.

example.q: A digital signature primarily guarantees:
example.solution: **Authenticity of the sender and integrity of the document** — the file cannot be altered unnoticed; it is not encryption for secrecy.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'A program that replicates itself is ___', 'which malware disguises as useful software', 'files locked for ransom' — behaviour described, malware named.
pyqPatterns.approach: Match the behaviour: needs a host file = virus; self-replicates alone = worm; disguised as useful software, no replication = trojan; locks files for money = ransomware; spies = spyware; records keystrokes = keylogger; shows ads = adware; army of zombie machines = botnet. The plant swaps virus and worm — check who needs the host.

example.q: Which type of malware spreads on its own through a network without a host file?
example.solution: Worm — viruses ride on host files; worms crawl the network independently.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A fraud scenario by e-mail, phone call, SMS, or a correct URL landing on a fake site — the attack's name is asked; 'full form / meaning of vishing, smishing'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Follow the channel: e-mail/fake site = phishing; phone call = vishing; SMS = smishing; correct address, fake destination = pharming; aimed at one chosen victim = spear phishing. All of them are social engineering — attacking the person, and the fix is never sharing OTP/PIN.

example.q: An SMS claiming your account will be blocked asks you to open a link and enter your bank password. This is:
example.solution: Smishing — phishing delivered by SMS; the link leads to a credential-stealing fake.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Which of these is NOT a security measure', 'which measure protects against ransomware', lists where one protection role is swapped (firewall cleaning viruses, antivirus filtering traffic).
pyqPatterns.approach: Fix the roles: firewall = filters network traffic by rules at the doorway; antivirus = scans and removes malware inside (needs updates); encryption = scrambles data (plaintext to ciphertext, AES, https padlock); 2FA = password + OTP/biometric; backups = the ransomware antidote. The plant: crediting the firewall with cleaning infections.

example.q: Which of the following does a firewall do?
example.solution: Filters incoming and outgoing network traffic by rules — it does not scan or clean files inside.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Hacking is punished under which section', 'identity theft section', 'which section was struck down', 'CERT-In works under ___', 'the IT Act was enacted in ___'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Memorise the ladder: 43 unauthorised access, 65 source code, 66 hacking, 66C identity theft, 66D online cheating, 67 obscenity, 72 privacy; 66A struck down in 2015 (Shreya Singhal). Act = 2000 (from 17 Oct, UNCITRAL-based, amended 2008). CERT-In under MeitY; NCIIPC guards critical infrastructure; helpline 1930.

example.q: Identity theft (misusing another's password or digital signature) is an offence under which section of the IT Act?
example.solution: Section 66C — added by the 2008 amendment.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Which statement about a salami attack / logic bomb / DoS is true', a scenario (tiny thefts, waiting code, flooded server, hidden listener) matched to its attack name.
pyqPatterns.approach: Anchor the classics: salami = many tiny thefts; data diddling = records changed at entry; logic bomb = code that waits for a trigger; SQL injection = commands typed into a form; DoS/DDoS = flooding (DDoS from many machines); MITM = secretly reading between two parties, typical on open Wi-Fi.

example.q: A malicious program lies dormant in a bank's system until 1 April and then deletes all records. This is a:
example.solution: Logic bomb — malware waiting for a trigger event before it detonates.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Scrambled data is called ___', 'https/padlock means ___', 'AES full form', 'strongest password' and 2FA meaning.
pyqPatterns.approach: Plaintext = readable, ciphertext = scrambled; decryption needs the key; AES = Advanced Encryption Standard; https + padlock = encrypted connection (TLS/SSL). Strong password = long, mixed characters, not personal; 2FA = password plus a second proof so a stolen password alone fails.

example.q: The padlock icon next to https:// in a browser indicates:
example.solution: The connection to that site is encrypted — data travels as unreadable ciphertext.

solvedExamples.q: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: A trojan horse replicates itself rapidly across networks
A worm needs a host file to attach itself to
A virus attaches to a host program and spreads when it is executed
Ransomware deletes files permanently without any demand
solvedExamples.solution: A virus lives inside a host file/program and activates on execution. Trojans do not self-replicate, worms need no host file, and ransomware encrypts files to demand ransom rather than simply deleting them.
solvedExamples.shortcut: The V-W-T triangle: Virus-vehicle, Worm-wanders, Trojan-tricks. Match each option's verb against it.

solvedExamples.q: A fraudster phones a user pretending to be a bank officer and asks for the OTP. This is an example of:
solvedExamples.solution: Voice-based fraud calls are vishing (voice phishing). Phishing uses fake e-mails/sites, smishing uses SMS, and pharming redirects browsers without any call or click.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Voice on the line = vishing. SMS = smishing. E-mail/site = phishing.

solvedExamples.q: Which section of the IT Act 2000 (post-2008 amendment) specifically deals with identity theft?
solvedExamples.solution: Section 66C punishes identity theft - fraudulent use of another person's password, digital signature or unique identification feature.
solvedExamples.shortcut: 66C = Credential/identity theft; 65 = source code; 67 = obscene content.

solvedExamples.q: The primary role of CERT-In is to:
options: Act as the national incident-response team for cyber security threats
solvedExamples.solution: CERT-In (Indian Computer Emergency Response Team, set up 2004 under MeitY) handles cyber-incident reporting, response, alerts and vulnerability management for India.
solvedExamples.shortcut: CERT = Computer Emergency Response Team - the name itself says incident response.

practice.q: Which malicious program can self-replicate across a network WITHOUT needing a host file or user action?
practice.solution: Worms travel and multiply on their own over network connections. Viruses need a host file, trojans need a user to install them and never self-replicate.
practice.shortcut: Worm = Wanders alone. If 'no host file / no user action' appears, it is a worm.

practice.q: A program that appears to be a free game but silently opens a backdoor for attackers is a:
practice.solution: The trojan's essence is disguise: useful-looking software that performs hidden malicious actions (backdoors, data theft). It does not self-replicate.
practice.shortcut: Looks useful, works evil = trojan horse.

practice.q: WannaCry, the global outbreak of May 2017 that encrypted systems and demanded bitcoin payments, was:
practice.solution: WannaCry was ransomware - it encrypted victims' files and demanded ransom (in bitcoin), spreading via the EternalBlue exploit against unpatched Windows.
practice.shortcut: Encrypt + demand money = ransomware; WannaCry is the stock example.

practice.q: A hardware or software component that records every key pressed on a keyboard to steal passwords is called a:
practice.solution: Keyloggers capture keystrokes (often as spyware/trojan payloads), exposing passwords and OTPs. A sniffer passively captures network packets instead.
practice.shortcut: Key-strokes recorded = keylogger; network packets read = sniffer.

practice.q: Sending e-mails that imitate a legitimate bank to trick users into revealing passwords is:
practice.solution: Phishing uses counterfeit messages/sites to 'fish' for credentials. Pharming needs no lure - DNS is poisoned so even correct URLs land on fake sites. Spamming is bulk unsolicited mail; defacement vandalises pages.
practice.shortcut: Fake mail asking for credentials = phishing, the umbrella term.

practice.q: In which attack is a user redirected to a fake website purely by corrupting DNS records, without clicking any link?
practice.solution: Pharming poisons the DNS/host entries so the genuine-looking domain resolves to the attacker's server - the user need do nothing wrong.
practice.shortcut: No click + fake site = pharming (phishing needs the victim's click).

practice.q: A Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attack works by:
options: Flooding a target server with traffic from many compromised machines
practice.solution: A botnet of 'zombie' systems swamps the target with requests so genuine users cannot be served. Nothing is encrypted (ransomware) or stolen directly - availability alone is attacked.

practice.q: An attacker who secretly relays and possibly alters communication between a user and a banking site is performing a:
practice.solution: In MITM the attacker sits between the two endpoints, intercepting/relaying traffic - a classic danger of unencrypted links and open Wi-Fi.
practice.shortcut: Secretly standing between two parties = man-in-the-middle.

practice.q: Entering a single quote followed by SQL code into a login form to manipulate the database is:
practice.solution: SQL injection feeds crafted SQL through input fields so the database executes attacker logic - usually a symptom of unvalidated input.

practice.q: Trying every possible character combination to guess a password is a:
practice.solution: Brute force exhausts all combinations; a dictionary attack tries only likely words from a list. Phishing and social engineering target people, not the algorithm.
practice.shortcut: Every combination = brute force; wordlist only = dictionary.

practice.q: Which of the following is primarily a PREVENTIVE network security tool that allows or blocks traffic based on defined rules?
practice.solution: A firewall inspects incoming/outgoing traffic against allow/deny rules and blocks unauthorised connections. Antivirus reacts to malware found in files.

practice.q: Requiring a password plus an OTP sent to the registered mobile is an example of:
practice.solution: Two-factor authentication combines two different evidence types - something you know (password) and something you receive (OTP). A leaked password alone then cannot breach the account.

practice.q: The Information Technology Act, which governs cyber activities in India, came into force in:
practice.solution: The IT Act was passed in 2000 (in force from 17 October 2000), based on the UNCITRAL model law; the 2008 amendment added identity theft (66C) and cyber terrorism (66F) provisions.

practice.q: Under the IT Act, cyber terrorism is dealt with in:
practice.solution: Section 66F covers cyber terrorism - acts threatening India's sovereignty, integrity or security through computers - punishable with imprisonment that may extend to life.

practice.q: The national helpline number for reporting online financial fraud in India is:
practice.solution: 1930 is the cybercrime financial-fraud helpline (paired with the cybercrime.gov.in portal) for fast freezing of defrauded money. 181 is the women's helpline, 1098 childline, 100 police.

practice.q: A program that attaches itself to a file and spreads when the file is shared and run is a —
practice.solution: **Virus** = needs a host file and a run to spread.

practice.q: Which malware can spread by itself across a network WITHOUT needing a host file?
practice.solution: **Worm** self-replicates standalone — no host, no user click needed.

practice.q: A 'free' PDF-reader downloaded from an unknown site secretly opens a backdoor for hackers. It does not copy itself. This is a —
practice.solution: **Trojan** — disguised as useful software and never self-replicates; the backdoor is its payload.

practice.q: Which statement is TRUE?
options: A worm needs a host file; a virus does not
A virus needs a host file; a worm does not
practice.solution: The classic distinction: **virus = host-dependent; worm = independent**; trojan never replicates at all.

practice.q: Malware that locks your files and demands money to release them is —
practice.solution: **Ransomware** holds data hostage — encrypt now, demand payment later (WannaCry, 2017).

practice.q: Which defence lets a ransomware victim recover WITHOUT paying?
practice.solution: Backups kept **offline** (disconnected) escape the encryption — restore instead of paying.

practice.q: WannaCry, which crippled systems worldwide in 2017, was an outbreak of —
practice.solution: **WannaCry (2017)** = the named ransomware epidemic exams quote.

practice.q: Which malware records every key pressed on a keyboard?
practice.solution: **Keylogger** captures keystrokes — passwords included — as you type.

practice.q: Software that quietly collects information about a user and sends it to a third party is —
practice.solution: **Spyware** spies — gathers your data in secret and ships it out.

practice.q: Programs that flood your screen with unwanted advertisements are called —
practice.solution: **Adware** = advertisement-software; annoying more than damaging.

practice.q: A network of infected computers remotely controlled by an attacker is a —
practice.solution: **Botnet** — an army of 'zombie' machines commanded together, owners unaware.

practice.q: Botnets are MOST commonly used to launch —
practice.solution: A botnet's muscle powers **DDoS floods and spam campaigns** — thousands of machines acting as one.

practice.q: Malware that hides deep in a system and conceals its own presence while giving an attacker administrator-level access is a —
practice.solution: **Rootkit** = root (admin) + kit — hides itself and hands over admin control.

practice.q: Fraudulent e-mails that look like your bank's and ask for your password are an example of —
practice.solution: **Phishing** — fishing for your credentials with fake bait mails/sites.

practice.q: Phishing carried out over a PHONE CALL is called —
practice.solution: **Vishing** = Voice phishing; SMS-based phishing is smishing.

practice.q: Phishing messages delivered by SMS are called —
practice.solution: **Smishing** = SMS phishing — the bait travels by text message.

practice.q: Sunil types his bank's web address CORRECTLY, but is still taken to a fake identical site that steals his login. This is —
practice.solution: **Pharming** — the address itself is hijacked (DNS poisoning); no user typing mistake occurred.
practice.shortcut: Pharming farms fakes at the address level.

practice.q: Flooding a server with useless requests so genuine users cannot use it is a —
practice.solution: **DoS** drowns the service — the goal is shutdown, not data theft.

practice.q: A DoS attack launched SIMULTANEOUSLY from thousands of hijacked computers is called —
practice.solution: **DDoS** = Distributed DoS — 'distributed' means many sources at once, usually a botnet.

practice.q: The army of hijacked machines that powers a DDoS flood is called a —
practice.solution: The DDoS muscle comes from a **botnet of zombie machines**.

practice.q: An attacker secretly positions himself between two parties and reads/alters their messages. This is a —
practice.solution: **MITM** — the hidden middleman between sender and receiver.

practice.q: Users of open public Wi-Fi are most exposed to which attack?
practice.solution: Unencrypted traffic on open Wi-Fi is read by anyone in the middle — **MITM territory**; HTTPS/VPN protect you.

practice.q: Which defence makes a man-in-the-middle attack ineffective?
practice.solution: With encryption the middleman intercepts only **ciphertext** he cannot read.

practice.q: A program hidden in a payroll system that waits for 1 April and then wipes the database is a —
practice.solution: **Logic bomb** — sleeps until its trigger condition (a date or event), then detonates.

practice.q: Stealing one rupee from each of ten lakh accounts is a —
practice.solution: **Salami slicing** — many tiny slices nobody notices, adding up to a fortune.

practice.q: Entering SQL commands into a website's input box to trick its database is —
practice.solution: **SQL injection** — hostile database commands injected through a form field.

practice.q: Changing figures in a record while they are being entered into a computer system is —
practice.solution: **Data diddling** = data altered before/during entry — the record itself lies.
practice.shortcut: Diddle the data at the door.

practice.q: A hardware or software barrier that filters traffic between your network and the Internet by rules is a —
practice.solution: **Firewall** = the rule-based doorman of a network.

practice.q: A firewall primarily decides —
options: Which network traffic to allow or block
practice.solution: Its whole job is **allow/block on traffic** passing the boundary — nothing about files or printing.

practice.q: Which statement about a firewall is TRUE?
options: It removes viruses from the hard disk
It replaces the need for backups
It filters the doorway but does not clean an infection inside
practice.solution: **Firewall filters traffic**; cleaning inside files is the antivirus's job.

practice.q: Software that scans the computer to find and remove viruses is —
practice.solution: **Antivirus** scans, detects and removes malware.

practice.q: Why must antivirus software be updated regularly?
options: New malware and new signatures appear every day
practice.solution: Antivirus matches **signatures**; without updates it cannot recognise yesterday's new malware.

practice.q: In an odd-one-out list, which item does NOT belong with the others?
practice.solution: Virus, trojan, worm are **malware (attacks)**; a firewall is **protection** — the odd one out.

practice.q: Two-factor authentication means —
options: Password plus a second proof such as an OTP
practice.solution: **2FA = something you know + something you have/are** — password plus OTP or fingerprint.

practice.q: Which is the STRONGEST password?
practice.solution: Long + mixed character types + not a personal fact = strong; the rest are the top of every 'worst passwords' list.

practice.q: A caller says he is from your bank and asks for the OTP you just received. You should —
options: Refuse — banks never ask for OTPs
Share it if he knows your name
practice.solution: **No genuine bank ever asks for OTP/PIN/CVV** — an OTP shared is money gone.

practice.q: Why does 2FA defeat a thief who has stolen your password?
options: He still lacks the second factor (OTP/biometric)
Stolen passwords work only on Fridays
practice.solution: 2FA's whole design: **knowing the password alone is not enough** — the second proof is missing.

practice.q: Readable, unscrambled data is called —
practice.solution: **Plaintext** = the readable original; scrambling turns it into ciphertext.

practice.q: Data scrambled into unreadable form is called —
practice.solution: **Ciphertext** = the encrypted form; decryption with the key returns plaintext.

practice.q: AES, the widely used modern encryption standard, expands to —
practice.solution: **AES = Advanced Encryption Standard** — the world's workhorse cipher.

practice.q: The padlock symbol with https:// in the browser's address bar means —
options: The connection to the site is encrypted
practice.solution: **https = HTTP inside an encrypted TLS/SSL tunnel** — the padlock certifies the tunnel, not the site's honesty.

practice.q: India's Information Technology Act was enacted in —
practice.solution: **IT Act, 2000** — in force from 17 October 2000.

practice.q: The IT Act, 2000 was based on the model law of —
practice.solution: **UNCITRAL** — the UN Commission on International Trade Law — recommended legal recognition of e-records.

practice.q: The IT Act received its major amendment in —
practice.solution: The **2008 amendment** (effective 2009) added 66C identity theft, 66D cheating, 66F cyber-terrorism and CERT-In's statutory role.

practice.q: Hacking (computer-related offences) is punished under which section of the IT Act?
practice.solution: **Sec 66** = computer-related offences — the 'hacking' section with dishonest intent.

practice.q: Tampering with computer source code is an offence under —
practice.solution: **Sec 65 = source code tampering**; 43 is unauthorised access/damage; 67 is obscenity.

practice.q: Which section of the IT Act was STRUCK DOWN by the Supreme Court in 2015?
practice.solution: **66A ('offensive messages') died in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015)** — free speech prevailed; the others remain live law.

practice.q: Publishing or transmitting obscene material in electronic form is punished under —
practice.solution: **Sec 67 = obscene electronic material** — 67A/67B variants were added in 2008.

practice.q: CERT-In, the agency that responds to cyber security incidents in India, works under —
practice.solution: **CERT-In functions under MeitY** (Ministry of Electronics and IT).

practice.q: Which body protects India's CRITICAL information infrastructure such as power grids and banking systems?
practice.solution: **NCIIPC** (under Sec 70A) guards critical infrastructure; CERT-In handles incident response generally.

practice.q: The national helpline number for reporting cyber fraud in India is —
practice.solution: **1930** — the national cyber-crime helpline (and cybercrime.gov.in online).

practice.q: A digital signature is created with the signer's —
options: Public key and verified with the private key
Private key and verified with the public key
practice.solution: **Sign with your private key; anyone verifies with your public key** — secrecy of the private key is everything.

practice.q: A digital signature mainly provides —
options: Authentication and integrity of the document
practice.solution: It proves **who signed** and that **nothing changed after signing** — not secrecy, not speed.

practice.q: Which section of the IT Act gives legal recognition to digital signatures?
practice.solution: **Sec 3 = authentication by digital (electronic) signature.**
